new_statements.quote: 3. There is contrastive pitch in Ocaina as seen in the following words (the acute accent over a vowel indicates high tone, whereas a vowel without such an accent indicates low tone): /xóótʸo/ your game bird; /xootʸo/ game bird; /tʸáxotʸo/ I sell it; /tʸaxotʸó/ I need to sell it [...] The following tone groups illustrate the two contrastive tone levels. In two syllable words there is contrast between high-low and low-low [...] In three syllable words there is contrast between low-low-low; low-high-low and high-low-low [...] Low tones are much more frequent in occurrence than high tones. Tone is involved in the morphophonemics of the language
new_statements.citation: Agnew, Arlene & Evelyn G. Pike. 1957. Phonemes of Ocaina (Huitoto). International Journal of American Linguistics 23(1): 24-27. doi:10.1086/464385
new_statements.locator: §3 'Tone', pp. 25-26 (PDF pages 2-3 of the Rosetta scan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., Rosetta Project scan, archive.org rosettaproject_oca_phon-1; pdfinfo title 'Ocaina Phonology'). Rendered PDF pages 2-3 (= IJAL XXIII pp. 25-26) and read the page images. Section '3.' begins at the foot of p. 25 col. 2 ('3. There is contrastive pitch in Ocaina') and continues on p. 26 col. 1: '(the acute accent over a vowel indicates high tone, whereas a vowel without such an accent indicates low tone): /xóótʸo/ your game bird; /xootʸo/ game bird; /tʸáxotʸo/ I sell it; /tʸaxotʸó/ I need to sell it; /ñonóóha/ kind of pod; /ñonooha/ wood worms. The following tone groups illustrate the two contrastive tone levels. In two syllable words there is contrast between high-low and low-l…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ocaina is described as a two-level tone language (high vs. low on each vowel/mora); the position of high tone is lexically and morphologically determined (any syllable, more than one syllable may be high, e.g. /xóótʸo/, /tʸaxotʸó/), and the article says nothing about stress. The complementary statement in Leach 1969 (Vocabulario ocaina p. 163) treats the same prominence as an accent: the written acute marks 'la sílaba o sílabas que llevan la mayor fuerza de voz', read at relatively high pitch; words with no accent are read low 'con acento menguante en la primera sílaba' (foojo 'la casa' vs fóójo 'tu casa'). So on both accounts the prominent syllable is lexically placed (unpredictable) and realized as high pitch, not positionally fixed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Agnew & Pike. Leach 1969 p. 163 notes only that words with no written accent are read with a low tone and a 'diminishing accent' on the first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone/accent is morphophonemic: it varies within paradigms (maaxa ~ mááxa- ~ maaxá- 'walk'), marks mode, tense and person (piixo 'axe' vs pïïxo 'your axe'), and accent shift forms plurals (Leach 1969 p. ~167; Fagua & Seifart 2010 p. 228) and some oblique case marking (Fagua & Seifart 2010 p. 234). Low tone downdrifts progressively through the utterance.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: tone contrasts are given on isolated words and on words inside short phrases (e.g.... óxï 'a lot'); Leach's statement concerns citation forms in a bilingual dictionary. Agnew & Pike's data: Peruvian Ocaina (Yaguasyacu, Ampiyacu, Algodón, Putumayo rivers, collected 1955-56); Leach: 'dialecto uvohsa' (speakers from La Chorrera, Colombia and Puerto Isango, Peru).
new_statements.identity_note: Both open primary sources describe Peruvian/Uvohsa Ocaina: Agnew & Pike 1957 (data from the Yaguasyacu, Ampiyacu, Algodón and Putumayo rivers, NE Peru, 1955-56) and Leach 1969/2008 ('dialecto uvohsa', consultants from La Chorrera, Colombia, and Puerto Isango, Peru). Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect nodes under ocai1244, so no separate glottocode applies; Fagua 2004/2013 also treat the uvohsa variety.

sources.note: Sec. 3 'Tone' (pp. 25-26): Ocaina has contrastive pitch with two tone levels (high, marked with acute; low unmarked); 2-syllable words contrast HL vs LL, 3-syllable words LLL, LHL, HLL; low tones far more frequent; tone is morphophonemic and marks mode/tense/person. The word 'stress' never appears; no stress statement. (Full 4-page article via Rosetta Project scan on archive.org; page images checked.)

sources.citation: Fagua Rincón, Doris & Frank Seifart. 2010. Aspectos morfosintácticos del ocaina: entre rasgos genéticos (familia Witoto) e influencias areales. Mundo Amazónico 1: 215-241.
sources.note: Morphosyntax only; annexes are IPA segment charts. States (p. 216) that published linguistic work on Ocaina is limited to a brief phonology (Agnew & Pike 1957), Pike 1961 and Leach 1969. Uses 'acento' (acute in orthography) without defining it as tone or stress: 'Una de ellas [estrategias de plural] es el cambio de la posición del acento' (p. 228, e.g. bou-rá-covo sg. vs bou-ra-cóvo pl.); some case marking 'por cambio de acento' (p. 234).

sources.citation: Leach, Ilo M. 1969. Vocabulario ocaina (Serie Lingüística Peruana 4). Yarinacocha: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano; 2nd ed. 2008, ed. Mary Ruth Wise, Lima: ILV. 'Aclaraciones acerca del alfabeto ocaina (dialecto uvohsa)', pp. 163-164; 'Notas gramaticales', pp. 165-173
sources.note: p. 163: 'El acento ortográfico ocaina se semeja al castellano, indicando la sílaba o sílabas que llevan la mayor fuerza de voz. Se lee la sílaba que lleva el acento ortográfico en tono relativamente elevado a las sílabas no acentuadas. Palabras sin acento ortográfico se leen con tono de voz relativamente bajo y con acento menguante en la primera sílaba: foojo la casa, fóójo tu casa.' I.e. the written accent marks the syllable(s) of greatest 'force of voice', realized as relatively high pitch; position is lexical (marked word by word, like Spanish orthography) and contrastive; unaccented words…
